name: Contemplation as the highest happiness
plain_explanation: Of all human activities, Aristotle holds that pure intellectual contemplation -- thinking for its own sake -- is the best and happiest, because it is most godlike and requires the least dependence on external circumstances.
precise_definition: Aristotle's culminating doctrine that perfect happiness lies in the best activity, contemplation, since it alone offers leisure and is 'preferable to war or politics or any other practical career'; the philosopher, being most akin to God in exercising reason, is 'the dearest to the gods' and therefore the happiest of men.
why_it_mattered: It is, in Russell's assessment, 'the only doctrine in the book which is not mere common sense,' distinguishing Aristotle's ethics from a merely conventional restatement of respectable Athenian opinion.
historical_origin: Set out near the close of the Nicomachean Ethics (Book X).
examples: The claim that 'the activity of God, which surpasses all others in blessedness, must be contemplative'
objections: Russell notes this doctrine sits awkwardly with the golden mean, since no vicious 'excess' of contemplation is identified
competing_positions: Practical, active life (politics, war) as the highest good, which Aristotle explicitly ranks below contemplation
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Links ethics to Aristotle's theology, since contemplation is the one respect in which men 'share in the divine life.'
